source.title: mOthello: When Do Cross-Lingual Representation Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer Emerge in Multilingual Models?
source.authors: Tianze Hua; Tian Yun; Ellie Pavlick

record.file_problem: none; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests when multilingual representations align and whether alignment alone suffices for transfer. Its results show alignment depends on training conditions and can be present without transfer; it uses a synthetic task and a probe-accuracy measure rather than the original claim's scaling or distance comparisons.
record.gate_note: The study measures cross-lingual alignment with probe accuracy across language types, anchor-token counts, layers, and training approaches. It also reports transfer performance, recorded separately as a finding not covered directly by the listed alignment versions. Results cited from prior work are not included. Table 3's probe-intervention errors are excluded because they validate probe interventions rather than measure representational convergence or transfer itself. Figure-based checkpoint curves and individual heatmap cells are summarized where the text gives an aggregate result.
record.test_reason: The study measures alignment between languages within a single multilingual model, not convergence between independently trained models. Different seeds repeat the within-model experiment; representations are never compared across seeds. Consequently, its alignment, training-condition and probe-sensitivity results do not test V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: naive multilingual pretraining fails to align representations across all languages within a model; anchor tokens encourage alignment, but alignment alone does not ensure cross-language transfer. Unified-output-space pretraining produces both in this synthetic task.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic multilingual Othello and cross-lingual board-state probe accuracy, rather than scaling models and comparing their induced distances. The study does not reproduce either cited original method.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment changes with anchor-token count, language-pair type, probe layer, number and arrangement of languages, and training approach (naive, anchor-token, or unified output space).

fits_no_version.finding: Naive multilingual training produces weak bilingual alignment and language clusters rather than alignment across all languages within a model; anchor tokens improve alignment, including indirectly connected language pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Languages within a multilingual Othello model need not share a common board-state representation; shared lexical anchors encourage such sharing.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-language probe accuracy varies by layer. Appendix A.5 additionally reports near-perfect color-flipped predictions in some split or compositional conditions and changes Table 1 scoring to the maximum of plain and color-flipped accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-language board-state alignment estimates depend on probe layer and whether color-permuted encodings count as aligned.

fits_no_version.finding: Anchor-trained models can have highly aligned language representations while target-language performance declines during source-language finetuning. Unified-output training yields both alignment and positive transfer, with weaker transfer for split and compositional pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-language representation alignment is insufficient for cross-language finetuning transfer in mOthello; the output objective affects whether transfer occurs.

record.problems: The evidence uses a toy synthetic task with fewer than 180 tokens per language and decoder-only GPT2-style models. The study itself notes that the setup is simpler than natural language and excludes encoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures. Several results are shown as plots without tabulated values; Table 1 reports averages across 3 seeds without stated error bars or other uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Individual heatmap cells and checkpoint-curve values from Figures 4–8 were not transcribed where the text gives only aggregate qualitative findings; the detailed intervention-error results in Table 3 were omitted because they validate probe interventions rather than directly measure the listed convergence versions. The paper also gives no separately stated textual result for the 100-language heatmap beyond the general cluster discussion.

untested.parts: No size or capability sweep measuring alignment between independently trained models.
No vision-language comparison or paired image-caption representations.
No comparison of learned representations across independently initialized networks; seed repetitions measure alignment between languages within each network.
No mapping, stitching or representation substitution between models. Probes are two-layer MLPs applied across languages within the same model.
No interpretable features or circuits compared across models.
No metric or input sensitivity analysis of between-model convergence. Layer choice and color-flip scoring concern within-model cross-language probing.
No completeness, plateau or causal explanation of between-model alignment. Shared anchors and output objectives are studied only for within-model cross-language alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Numerical table entries match the supplied text. The principal extraction error is treating within-model cross-language alignment as between-model convergence. All cannot_determine states refer to the listed claim versions, not uncertainty about the reported within-model results. Appendix A.5's scoring adjustment should accompany Table 1 when those results are presented.

versions.untested_parts: No model scale or capability sweep and no comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representations.
Random initializations are considered for language alignment, but the study does not test shared features or subspaces across seeds of independently trained networks.

The cross-lingual probes transfer across language inputs within one model; the study does not test mapping representations between models, layer stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are measured.
It varies input language forms, anchor-token counts, training approach, and probe layer, but does not compare alternative similarity metrics, neighbour settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Tests alignment under a controlled synthetic language task and training variants; does not establish whether shared data or objectives explain alignment in natural-language models.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Language-pair types and anchor-token counts in Table 1; probe layers in Table 2; training approaches and language variants in Figures 5–6
reader_labels.reason: Alignment varies substantially with anchor count and layer, and differs across language types and training setups (r1-r21, r24-r35). The study does not test alternative similarity metrics or OOD inputs.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Naive multilingual pretraining and the indirect-anchor experiments
reader_labels.reason: Naive training yields language clusters rather than alignment across all languages, while anchor-connected languages can align indirectly (r22-r23, r36-r41).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Alignment can become near-perfect or well established under these specific training conditions, so incomplete alignment is not universal across the tested setups (r10-r12, r30-r35).
